Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

deny verb

say that something is not true

also denial, I don’t deny it, deny that, deny doing it, I won’t deny it

classical

Ter. Ad. 799: Factum est; nōn negō.
Cic. Fin. 2.68 (Lewis & Short): Stōicī negant quidquam esse bonum, nisi quod honestum sit

negō, negāre, negāvī, negātum

verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, or an accusative and infinitive · Conjugation on Wiktionary

deny, say that … not

The opposite of ajō, to say yes (see say). “He denies he did it” is negat sē fēcisse: Latin puts the negative in the verb and leaves the infinitive positive. The same verb refuses (see deny, refuse).

Other words

  • īnfitior, īnfitiārī, īnfitiātus sum — deny, disown; refuse to own a debt

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. Cat. 3.11 (Lewis & Short): cum id posset īnfitiārī, repentē cōnfessus est; Traupman 302 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    To deny what one is charged with, the opposite of fatērī; in law, to deny a debt or a deposit (Lewis & Short).

  • īnfitiās eō — deny

    phrase: the accusative īnfitiās with forms of īre · also used · classical · Plaut. Curc. 489: Nēmō it īnfitiās.; Ter. Ad. 339: ille īnfitiās ībit, sat sciō

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; in prose Nep., Liv., not Cic.)

    Mostly with a negative: nēmō it īnfitiās, no one denies it; neque negō neque īnfitiās eō (Liv. 6.40.4). Lewis & Short: not in Cicero or Caesar.

  • nōn īnfitior — I don’t deny it

    also used · classical · Traupman 146

    The verb is classical (Cicero, Livy); with a negative it admits a point.

Examples

  • Negat quis? negō: ait? ajō.

    Someone says no? I say no. He says yes? I say yes.Ter. Eun. 252

  • Factum est; nōn negō.

    It’s done; I don’t deny it.Ter. Ad. 799

  • Nēmō it īnfitiās.

    No one denies it.Plaut. Curc. 489

See also say, deny, lie, true.
